summary: Describes a simple way to make link state routing protocols treat a broadcast network as a point-to-point connection. Choosing the right circuit type matters for adjacency formation, flooding, and how the network appears in the topology. Treating a two-router LAN as point-to-point can simplify things. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If just two people share a long table, they can talk directly instead of shouting across the room. This lets two routers on a shared network behave that way, which is simpler.

questions: link state point to point lan
how to treat a lan as point-to-point in ospf
does ospf need a designated router on a two router lan
subtitle: How to tell OSPF or IS-IS to treat a LAN link between two routers as a plain point-to-point link.

tldr.problem: Link state protocols treat a LAN as a broadcast circuit, with a designated router and a virtual node in the topology, even when only two routers share it. That adds overhead without the benefits.
tldr.mechanism: A configuration setting tells the routing protocol the circuit is point-to-point whatever the media is, so it sends and expects point-to-point protocol packets over the LAN. The RFC also covers address resolution and detection of misconfiguration.
tldr.outcome: The link behaves like a point-to-point link, which removes DR/DIS election and the pseudonode. Both routers must be configured the same way, or adjacencies will not form.

today: RFC 5309 is an Informational document from October 2008, and the registry shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Treat a LAN as Point-to-Point
sections.content:
IS-IS and OSPF handle point-to-point and broadcast circuits differently for adjacencies, flooding and topology. Broadcast circuits use a designated router and show up in the topology as virtual nodes (a pseudonode in IS-IS, a network LSA in OSPF). Point-to-point circuits have neither, and for IS-IS they need no periodic database synchronization.

Sometimes only two routers share a LAN: the media is used for long-haul point-to-point operation, there are only two routers on the physical LAN, or only two on a virtual LAN (vLAN). Treating the link as a broadcast circuit then adds overhead without benefit. Treating it as point-to-point lets the routers skip DR/DIS election, flood as on p2p links without OSPF LSA reflection or periodic IS-IS CSNPs, and advertise only the connection between the two routers. An ISP can also split a LAN into several vLANs to assign different costs to IGP neighbors, and the IGP can view them as a mesh of point-to-point connections.
sections.eli5: Two kids at a big table do not need a monitor to pass notes. Dropping the monitor saves work.

sections.title: How the Mechanism Works
sections.content:
The idea is simple: add a configuration option that tells the IGP the circuit type is point-to-point, irrespective of media. The IGP sends protocol packets with point-to-point information and expects to receive them that way. Over LAN media, the MAC header must carry the correct multicast MAC address, and in a vLAN environment the proper vLAN ID.

For IS-IS, the packets are still IS-IS LAN packets at the link layer. The multi-destination addresses AllISs, AllL1ISs and AllL2ISs can be used, and AllISs is recommended. The point-to-point IIH (IS-IS Hello) MUST include the IP interface addresses: the interface address for a numbered interface, the interface-independent address for an unnumbered one, and link-local addresses for IPv6.

For OSPF and OSPFv3, routers should support an interface setting for the topology type. Both routers join the AllSPFRouters multicast group (224.0.0.5 for OSPF, FF02::5 for OSPFv3) and send all OSPF packets to it, as on a physical point-to-point link in RFC 2328.
sections.eli5: You just flip a switch that says this is a two-person line. The routers then talk the way they would on a private wire.

sections.title: Next Hops, ARP and ND
sections.content:
On a real point-to-point link a router needs no next-hop address, so the link can be unnumbered and borrow an address from another interface. A LAN differs: the IP next hop is not optional, because the router needs it to find the neighbor's MAC address. The next hop has to be a valid interface or internal address on the adjacent router.

ARP therefore must be able to resolve the internal IPv4 address used on an unnumbered p2p-over-lan circuit, which means relaxing the check that the source address of an ARP request matches the local subnet. For IPv6, Neighbor Discovery resolves the MAC for the link-local address. Where that is not possible, the RFC lists static configuration of the MAC address and MAC address gleaning, taking the neighbor's MAC from a frame carrying a routing protocol packet.
sections.eli5: Even on a two-person line, the routers still need to know each other's street address to deliver mail, so they have to find it out.

sections.title: Catching Misconfiguration
sections.content:
Because only configuration separates a LAN circuit from a point-to-point one, early detection of misconfiguration matters. A point-to-point circuit that receives LAN hellos MUST discard them, and a LAN circuit that receives point-to-point hellos MUST discard them. If the system ID or router ID in a hello does not match the established adjacency, the packet MUST be discarded.

If OSPF hello suppression ([RFC1793], RFC 1793) is active, it MUST be terminated for a period of RouterIntervalSeconds, after which the adjacency will time out and may form with a neighbor that has a different router ID, or suppression may be renegotiated. Implementations should log and offer debugging information about these events.
sections.eli5: If one kid thinks it is a two-person line and the other thinks it is a big table, they ignore each other until someone fixes it.

sections.title: Compatibility, Scale and Security
sections.content:
Both routers must support the extension and both must configure the segment as a p2p-over-lan circuit. Both SHOULD support at least one of the listed methods for mapping IP addresses to MAC addresses, and if one router uses a proprietary method, both must be able to use it. Otherwise the link should be configured as a standard LAN link.

The trade-off is scale. Splitting a LAN into several vLANs and using this extension gives up the inherent scalability of multi-access networks, and in general increases the link state database size, the flooding, and the route calculation overhead. Unnumbered LAN links also inherit a serial-link problem: a specific interface between routers cannot be pinged or monitored.

The RFC says it introduces no new security issues for IS-IS, OSPF, ARP or ND. If the two routers disagree on circuit type, adjacencies never form, with no fallback except a manual configuration change.
sections.eli5: It saves work on tiny two-person tables, but if you split a big room into many tiny tables, you end up with more to keep track of.
